trace.topic: Your VCs Are Worried About Public Multiples. Do You Need To Worry, Too?
trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should explain that public multiples matter because they shape private funding expectations and exit math.
It should distinguish between what founders can control and what they cannot.
It should advise founders to focus on fundamentals rather than obsessing over market chatter.
rubric_must_haves: Provides practical founder guidance, not just investor commentary.
Includes at least one example of how multiples affect fundraising, burn, or planning.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should say that founders cannot ignore public multiples because they influence valuation, fundraising, and investor psychology, but they also should not let them run the company. The right move is to understand the implications, tighten execution, and build the kind of business that works under tougher market assumptions.
trace.prompt:
Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: Your VCs Are Worried About Public Multiples. Do You Need To Worry, Too?

Style examples from train-owned source text.
Use them for voice only. They are not evidence for claims.
Do not copy long passages verbatim.
[Style 1]
Dear SaaStr: How Can You Ensure a Smooth Transition When A New Team Member Takes Over a Customer Account?
Add value in the first interaction.  This is so rare.
There’s nothing more frustrating than getting a random email, “Hi, Tony is gone from the company. I know nothing about you, but I’m your new rep. Can we schedule a call?”
Find some way to add value.
One great way is to demo upcoming features / an upcoming release.
“Hi, I’m Jason, your next account exec. I’d love to find a way to help even more. Can I show you or anyone on your team the new AI features we’re launching shortly? There’s no additional cost for them and based on what I can see, they may radically increase your efficiency.”
Not perfect. But much better.
A second, albeit riskier, way to add value is to set up a call asking for “honest feedback on how we’re doing.”
This works, too.  Customers often just want to be heard.  The “problem” is you might have to do something about it.
[Style 2]
Dear SaaStr: When Is It Too Soon to Target Enterprise Customers in SaaS?
It too soon to target enterprise clients when you can’t support their needs 90 days
after
you close them.
It’s sort of OK in the enterprise to promise features and functionality that are sort of there … so long as you deliver them fairly promptly after the deal closes.
In fact, it happens all the time. Enterprise customers will even sign contracts agreeing to buy so long as you implement a key feature with X number of days.
But if you don’t have the team, commitment and experience to deliver that functionality at least X days after you close a Big Customer … you aren’t ready.  They’ll churn or at least, never fully deploy.
You don’t have to have the full enterprise package in the early days to close enterprise customers, especially if they have interest in you.  You’ll get some slack as a new, emerging vendor.  Especially if you have a strong deployment team.
But you have to meet your commitments and promises to them fairly soon after the deal closes.

trace.answer: Your VCs Are Worried About Public Multiples. Do You Need To Worry, Too?
trace.raw_model_output:
So public multiples have fallen significantly since Q2’22. We’ve seen that before. And in the end, it doesn’t matter — as long as your start-up is growing well.
First, remember the markets go through cycles
.  We had crazy valuations in late 2020-early 2021, then dropped -50%+, and now are back down again.  That’s natural.
Second, public multiples are still pretty darn high by historical standards
. So while yes, this may make VC funding harder, and yes, it does mean founders won’t raise quite as many rounds as they did at peak times … those same issues existed during all prior downturns.
Third, private market valuations remain higher than ever
. If anything, that’s where the real pressure is right now.  Yes, things may seem tougher for startups today.  But if you have a good business and happy customers — you probably really don’t need to worry so much about public market multiples.
Fourth, most of us would rather sell our companies today than wait a few years
. In fact, a survey of 100+ top tech CEOs found half were considering selling. Why? Because the best offers may be coming later, but we already got 10x+ revenue multiples. Those offers likely won’t come again.
And finally, let me share one piece of data that tells you everything you need to know:
At the 2019
SaaStr Annual,
our speakers averaged 18 months from founding to $1m ARR. Today, they average 12 months. Not 24 months, like in 2022. Or 30 months, like pre-pandemic. But 12 months. One year.
That’s not because the product is any different. It’s not because the market has changed. It’s not because of COVID.
